title: DTP and VTP
summary: Two Cisco proprietary protocols: DTP, which negotiates whether a port becomes an access or trunk port, and VTP, which synchronises the VLAN database across switches — plus why both should usually be disabled.

content.body: DTP and VTP were removed from the CCNA 200-301 exam topics list. You still need to understand what they do — questions about them can still appear — but a basic overview is enough. Do not study them to the depth of 802.1Q.

**DTP** is a Cisco proprietary protocol that lets Cisco switches dynamically determine whether an interface becomes an **access port** or a **trunk port**, without manual configuration.

In short: two Cisco switches connected together can negotiate a trunk; otherwise the interface becomes an access port.

- DTP is **enabled by default** on all Cisco switch interfaces.
- Because it is proprietary, it only works between Cisco switches.
- Using DTP means you never have to type `switchport mode access` or `switchport mode trunk`.

**But for security, DTP should be disabled on all switchports and ports configured manually.** DTP can be exploited by attackers.

The modes are configured with `switchport mode dynamic`, which offers two options:

- **`dynamic desirable`** — *actively* tries to form a trunk with the neighbour.
- **`dynamic auto`** — *passive*. It will not initiate, but says in effect "if you want a trunk, I'll form one".

sections.title: DTP outcome matrix — resulting operational mode

content.body:
`show interfaces g0/0 switchport` is the command that reveals what DTP actually did:

- **Switchport: Enabled** — this is a Layer 2 port. A routed port (`no switchport`) would show differently.
- **Administrative Mode** — what you *configured*, e.g. `dynamic desirable`.
- **Operational Mode** — what the port is *actually doing*, e.g. `trunk` or `static access`.
- **Administrative Trunking Encapsulation** / **Operational Trunking Encapsulation** — configured vs negotiated encapsulation.
- **Negotiation of Trunking** — whether DTP frames are being sent. `On` for dynamic desirable, dynamic auto and trunk modes; `Off` for access mode or after `switchport nonegotiate`.

**`static access`** means an access port belonging to a single VLAN that does not change. (There are also *dynamic access* ports where a server assigns the VLAN by MAC address, but that is out of scope for the CCNA.)

Two important behaviours:

- **DTP will never form a trunk with a router, PC or other non-Cisco-switch device** — the port stays in access mode. So for router on a stick you **must** manually configure the switch port as a trunk.
- Manually configuring a trunk with `switchport mode trunk` does **not** stop DTP frames being sent. Only `switchport nonegotiate` (or `switchport mode access`) does that.

rows: `switchport mode dynamic desirable` — they actively try to trunk
`switchport nonegotiate` stops DTP frames being sent
Also disables DTP negotiation and stops DTP frames
Does NOT stop DTP frames — add `switchport nonegotiate` too
Default is `switchport trunk encapsulation negotiate`. If both switches support it, **ISL is favoured** over dot1Q
VLAN 1 when using ISL; the native VLAN when using dot1Q (VLAN 1 by default)

content.body:
**VTP** is another Cisco proprietary protocol. It lets you configure VLANs on a central **server** switch; other switches (**clients**) then synchronise their VLAN database to it, so you do not have to create every VLAN on every switch.

It is designed for large networks with many VLANs — but like DTP it is rarely used today, and the recommendation is **not** to use it.

There are three versions (1, 2, 3). Most modern Cisco switches support all three; older ones may only support 1 and 2.

**Critically: VTP only synchronises the VLAN database.** It does *not* assign interfaces to VLANs. You still configure `switchport access vlan 10` on every switch individually.

rows: Yes — servers also act as clients, syncing to a higher revision number
Yes, to the highest revision number in its domain
Yes, but only locally — never advertised
Yes, but only for its own domain

sections.title: Revision numbers and the VTP danger

content.body:
The **configuration revision number** is the heart of VTP. Every time a VTP server adds, modifies or deletes a VLAN, it increments the revision number. **The highest revision number wins** — it is considered the newest, most accurate VLAN database, and every switch in the domain synchronises to it.

Other rules:

- VTP advertisements are sent on **trunk ports only**, never on access ports.
- If a switch with **no VTP domain** (domain NULL) receives an advertisement carrying a domain name, it **automatically joins that domain**.
- VTP servers also act as clients, so a server will happily overwrite its own database from another server with a higher revision number.

**The danger.** Suppose your production domain `cisco` is at revision 5 with VLANs 1, 10, 20, 30 and 40. You plug in an old spare switch from storage that has the same domain name, revision **50**, and VLANs 1, 99 and 220. Its advertisements are forwarded across the whole domain, every switch synchronises to it, and **every host in VLANs 10, 20, 30 and 40 instantly loses connectivity.**

This is the main reason VTP is avoided in modern networks.

**Two ways to reset the revision number to 0** before connecting an old switch:

1. Change the VTP domain to an **unused domain name**.
2. Change the VTP mode to **transparent**.

steps.narration: All four switches start with default settings: VTP server mode, domain NULL, revision 0, five default VLANs.
On SW1: `vtp domain cisco`, then create VLAN 10 named ENGINEERING. The revision number increases to 1 and SW1 advertises out its trunks.
SW2 had domain NULL, so it automatically joins domain `cisco` and syncs its VLAN database. `show vlan brief` now lists VLAN 10 — with no configuration on SW2 at all.
SW3 is set to transparent mode with domain `juniper`. It does NOT sync, and because the domain differs it does not forward the advertisement either. Its revision resets to 0.
SW4 is left behind — no VLAN 20, still on the old revision number.
Change SW3's domain back to `cisco`. It still refuses to sync its own database, but it now forwards advertisements — and SW4 catches up with SW1 and SW2.

rows: Which versions the switch supports vs which it is using (version 1 by default)
NULL by default. All switches must share a domain name to synchronise
1005 with VTP v1/v2 — the extended range 1006–4094 requires **VTP version 3**
5 on a default switch: VLAN 1 plus 1002–1005
0 on a default switch; increments on every VLAN add/modify/delete. Highest wins

content.body:
Change the version with the `vtp version` command. Doing so increases the revision number, and other servers and clients then sync and switch to the new version too.

Cisco's own summary of the difference between v1 and v2: *"VTP V2 is not much different than VTP V1. The major difference is that VTP V2 introduces support for Token Ring VLANs. If you use Token Ring VLANs, you must enable VTP V2. Otherwise, there is no reason to use VTP V2."*

Token Ring is obsolete, so in practice there is no reason to use version 2. Version 3 has many more features — including extended VLAN range support — but is well beyond the scope of the CCNA.

For VTP, know: its purpose, the difference between server / client / transparent mode, that switches are in server mode by default, that servers also act as clients, and how revision numbers decide which database wins. For DTP, know the mode matrix, that newer switches default to dynamic auto and older ones to dynamic desirable, and that DTP never forms a trunk with a router.

commands.description: Sets the port to actively negotiate a trunk using DTP. It forms a trunk with a neighbour set to trunk, dynamic desirable or dynamic auto.
commands.note: This was the default mode on older Cisco switches.

commands.description: Sets the port to passively wait for DTP negotiation. It forms a trunk only if the neighbour is trunk or dynamic desirable; two auto ports stay as access ports.
commands.note: This is the default mode on most modern Cisco switches.

commands.description: Disables DTP on the port so it stops sending negotiation frames. The port keeps whatever static mode it was given.
commands.note: Recommended practice: configure trunks and access ports statically and turn DTP off. Note that a router never negotiates a trunk.

commands.description: Lets the two switches agree on the trunk encapsulation automatically. If both support ISL, ISL is chosen in preference to 802.1Q.

commands.example:
SW1# show interfaces g0/0 switchport
Administrative Mode: dynamic auto
Operational Mode: static access
commands.description: Reveals both the configured (administrative) mode and the resulting negotiated (operational) mode — the way to confirm what DTP actually decided.

Sets the switch's VTP role. Servers can create and modify VLANs and advertise them; clients accept advertisements but cannot edit VLANs; transparent switches keep their own local VLAN database and simply forward advertisements.
Sets the VTP domain name. Switches only exchange VTP information when their domain names match.
commands.note: A switch with a NULL (unset) domain automatically joins the first domain it hears an advertisement from.

commands.description: Protects the VTP domain so only switches with the matching password accept its advertisements.
Selects the VTP version. Version 3 is required to advertise extended-range VLANs (1006-4094).

commands.example:
SW1# show vtp status
VTP Operating Mode: Server
Configuration Revision: 4
commands.description: Displays the VTP mode, domain, version and — critically — the configuration revision number.
commands.note: The switch with the highest configuration revision number wins. Adding an old switch with a high revision number can wipe the VLAN database of the entire domain.

questions.question: SW1 and SW2 are both new switches whose connected interfaces operate as access ports. SW2 fails and is replaced with an old spare switch, reset before connecting. A trunk unexpectedly forms. Why?
questions.explanation: Older switches default to `dynamic desirable`, which actively tries to form a trunk. SW1, being new, defaults to `dynamic auto`, which will accept a trunk when the other side initiates. Desirable + auto = trunk.

options.label: A
options.text: Interfaces on old switches default to switchport mode trunk

options.label: B
options.text: Interfaces on old switches default to switchport mode dynamic desirable

options.label: C
options.text: Access ports are a feature of newer switches only

options.label: D
options.text: The old switch had a higher VTP revision number

questions.question: SW1–SW2–SW3 are connected in a line. You want SW2 to forward SW1's VLAN database information to SW3, but you do not want SW2 to synchronise its own VLAN database to SW1. Which command should you use on SW2?
questions.explanation: A switch in VTP transparent mode forwards VTP advertisements within its own domain but does not synchronise its own VLAN database, and does not advertise its own database either.

options.label: A
options.text: vtp mode transparent

options.label: B
options.text: vtp transparent mode

options.label: C
options.text: vlan mode transparent

options.label: D
options.text: vtp mode client

questions.question: What are TWO methods to reset a switch's VTP revision number to 0? (Each is a complete solution.)
questions.explanation: Changing the VTP domain to an unused name, or switching the device into VTP transparent mode, both reset the revision number to 0. This is essential before connecting an old switch to a VTP network.

options.label: A
options.text: Change the VTP domain to an unused domain name

options.label: B
options.text: Change the switch to VTP server mode

options.label: C
options.text: Change the switch to VTP transparent mode

options.label: D
options.text: Use the `vtp reset` command

questions.question: Two switch ports are both left in `dynamic auto` mode. What is the resulting operational mode?
questions.explanation: Neither side actively initiates a trunk in dynamic auto mode, so no trunk forms and both ports operate as access ports in VLAN 1.

options.label: A
options.text: Trunk

options.label: B
options.text: Access ports in VLAN 1

options.label: C
options.text: The link is err-disabled

options.label: D
options.text: One becomes a trunk and the other an access port

questions.question: You are configuring router on a stick. Can you leave the switch port facing the router in `dynamic desirable` mode?
questions.explanation: DTP never forms a trunk with a router, PC or other non-switch device — the port would simply become an access port. The trunk must be configured manually.

options.label: A
options.text: Yes — the router will negotiate a trunk via DTP

options.label: B
options.text: No — DTP does not form trunks with routers, so the trunk must be configured manually

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, but only if the router runs VTP

options.label: D
options.text: No — the port must be in dynamic auto mode instead

questions.question: Which statement about VTP is correct?
questions.explanation: VTP synchronises only the VLAN database. Assigning interfaces to VLANs (`switchport access vlan 10`) is still done switch by switch.

options.label: A
options.text: VTP also assigns switch interfaces to their VLANs automatically

options.label: B
options.text: VTP synchronises only the VLAN database; interface assignment is still manual on each switch

options.label: C
options.text: VTP advertisements are sent on access ports as well as trunk ports

options.label: D
options.text: VTP clients can create VLANs as long as they are in the same domain
